source: Northern Territory Government, Department of Resources — Field Guide to Pests, Beneficials, Diseases and Disorders of Mangoes (2nd edition), December 2010, ISBN 978-0-7245-7200-7
text:
Insect action levels for the Northern Territory (Australia). The action level is the pest population density at which control is recommended. To determine action levels, survey 10-20 trees per hectare (or per 100 trees), per the orchard monitoring procedure.
- Mango leafhopper: examine flower panicles, or new terminal shoots in the months leading up to flowering. Control if there is 1 or more per orchard; in low populations, only spray affected trees.
- Mango planthopper: examine terminals and fruit stalks. Control if 10% of terminals or fruit stalks are infested.
- Redbanded thrips: examine leaves. Control if 10% of terminals are infested.
- Dimpling bug: examine flower panicles. Apply treatment when there are 2 or more bugs per 4 trees.
- Flower-eating caterpillars: examine flowers and pull apart webbing to look for live caterpillars. Control when there are 2 or more per flower panicle.
- Mango scale: examine 4-5 terminals per tree, looking for live females and crawlers. Immature females and crawlers are the easiest to control; mature females are difficult to control. Control when susceptible, before flowering and before harvest.
- Mango tip borer: examine terminals. Control if 10% of terminals are infested.
- Mango seed weevil: examine golf-ball-size fruit for egg-laying blemishes with leaking sap. Control if there are egg-laying blemishes on fruit on more than 2 trees per 100 trees. When exporting fruit, refer to quarantine requirements.
- Fruit spotting bug and tea mosquito bug: examine new shoots and small fruit for bugs and damage. Control when there is fresh feeding damage or 1-2 bugs per tree; spot-spray affected trees and nearby trees.
- Fruit flies: monitor with CUE lure traps to get an idea of population (traps only capture male flies). Control as per Interstate Certification Assurance (ICA) requirements.
- Longicorn beetle: check for dying shoots (yellowing leaves) or branches. Treat all affected trees; prune and destroy affected branches. Sprays may assist control.
- Giant northern termite: to detect activity, drill a hole about 12 mm in diameter into the centre of the trunk at waist height - if termites are active they will seal the hole with mud within 24 hours. Ring-barking, termite mud on trunk/branches, and folded hollow branches are also signs of activity. Trees can be treated by trunk or soil injection, or termites can be aggregated in aggregation drums and treated once highly active (up to six weeks); contact the relevant plant protection authority for termiticide details.
- Mango fruit borer: look for holes and extruded frass (insect droppings) on developing fruit, including fallen fruit.
caveat: This source is an Australian (Northern Territory) government field guide, not a Cambodia-specific MAFF publication. It is included as a supplementary international reference for visual identification and general pest/disease biology only. Species presence, seasonal timing (the guide's monthly monitoring calendars reflect the NT dry/wet season cycle), and any pesticide or chemical guidance are specific to northern Australia and may not apply directly to Cambodian conditions, seasons, or registered products. This edition of the source itself does not list specific pesticide products or rates (noted as intentionally omitted pending updated registrations), so none are reported here either.
